slides.title: Earn Trust Before You Amplify
slides.subtitle: How useful participation becomes recognition and trust
slides.transcript:
Module one: Earn Trust Before You Amplify.

Building a brand in the OCP Community starts in a different place from a traditional marketing campaign. It starts with useful participation. People notice the teams that listen carefully, share real expertise, and help the Community solve problems.

In this module, you'll learn how that work becomes credibility. We'll look at the trusted environment OCP protects, how to enter a project workstream thoughtfully, the many forms a contribution can take, and why collaboration creates more value than promotion alone. Let's get started.

slides.title: A Two-Part Brand-Building Playbook
slides.subtitle: Earn credibility first. Then choose the right way to extend its reach.
slides.media_embed:
Dirk Van Slyke
Chief Marketing Officer, Open Compute Project

figure.alt: Dirk Van Slyke, OCP Chief Marketing Officer.
figure.caption: Course source presenter.

slides.transcript:
This course grows out of a presentation delivered in April 2025 by Dirk Van Slyke, Chief Marketing Officer for the OCP Foundation. Dirk has spent years helping organizations understand how to participate well and how to turn meaningful Community work into earned recognition.

We'll follow that practical path in two parts. First, we'll focus on earning trust through listening, participation, contribution, and collaboration. Then we'll look at the channels that can extend the reach of useful work, including the Marketplace, events, communications, and OCP Academy.

The full course takes about twenty-six minutes. You can also watch Dirk's original presentation from the resource link. His contact email appears again at the end if you want to continue the conversation.

slides.title: This Is Not Pay-for-Play
slides.subtitle: Trust grows when people can collaborate without being treated as sales leads.

bullets.text: Engineers come together to solve challenges in an open environment.
Useful participation matters more than promotional spend.
OCP does not sell Community contact information.
What you get out reflects what you put into the Community.

figure.alt: A trusted OCP Community space containing useful participation, open collaboration, and room to solve hard problems; sales-first behavior remains outside.
figure.caption: The trusted environment works when participation and collaboration serve the shared problem—not a sales funnel.

entries.text: Trust creates room to solve hard problems
Sales-first behavior does not belong here

slides.transcript:
The first principle is simple: OCP is a Community where engineers come together to solve challenges in a safe and trusted environment.

That trust depends on clear boundaries. OCP isn't a pay-for-play channel, and it isn't a place where spending money buys editorial attention or technical influence. The Foundation also doesn't sell Community contact information. Participants should be able to collaborate without wondering whether every conversation will turn into an unsolicited sales approach.

This changes how an organization should think about brand building. The goal isn't to push a message at the Community. The goal is to become known for helping the Community make progress. A sponsorship can create visibility, and membership can show commitment, but neither one substitutes for useful behavior.

Dirk's phrase captures the point: "You get out of it what you put into it." The return comes from the quality of your participation, not simply the size of a budget. When your team consistently listens, contributes, and treats people with respect, recognition follows the work. That is the foundation for every channel we'll discuss later.

slides.title: Participation Builds Credibility
slides.subtitle: Open collaboration connects technical progress with durable brand trust.

cards.title: Innovate
cards.body: Help shape emerging technology roadmaps.

cards.title: Connect
cards.body: Work with industry-wide engineering and research teams.

cards.title: Accelerate
cards.body: Advance open standards and reduce time to market.

cards.title: De-risk
cards.body: Build options that can reduce supply-chain exposure.

cards.title: Earn trust
cards.body: Let useful work demonstrate technical leadership.

cards.title: Sustain
cards.body: Support efficiency, circularity, and responsible infrastructure.

slides.transcript:
Open participation creates several kinds of value at the same time.

Your engineers can help shape emerging technology roadmaps instead of waiting for those roadmaps to arrive. They can connect with peers across the industry and gain access to a wider pool of engineering and research and development experience. That shared context can help teams identify better approaches sooner.

Collaboration can also accelerate open standards and reduce time to market. When an industry agrees on adaptable interfaces, requirements, or best practices, organizations gain more choices. Those choices can reduce supply-chain risk and make it easier for a broader ecosystem to build compatible solutions.

The brand benefit is real, but it is the result rather than the starting pitch. People learn which teams bring evidence, which teams follow through, and which teams help others succeed. Over time, that behavior becomes technical credibility and trust.

OCP also connects innovation with efficiency, circularity, and sustainability. A contribution that helps the Community build better infrastructure can create value well beyond the organization that first proposed it. That is the power of working in the open.

slides.title: Listen First in Project Workstreams
slides.subtitle: Relevance and patience come before visibility.

bullets.text: Identify projects and workstreams connected to your organization's expertise.
Join regular calls with the people who can help solve the technical problem.
Listen for priorities, constraints, decision patterns, and existing relationships.
Contribute where your experience can move shared work forward.
Consider volunteer leadership after trust and momentum are established.

figure.alt: Five-step sequence: find the relevant workstream, join and listen, learn priorities and context, offer useful help, and lead after trust is established.
figure.caption: Visibility is the result of the sequence, not the first step.

slides.transcript:
Project workstreams are usually the best place to begin because that is where the Community's real problems are discussed.

Start by identifying the projects and workstreams most relevant to your organization's expertise. Then involve the engineers, operators, or specialists who can understand the details and contribute to the work. This isn't a job for a marketing representative looking for a place to insert a product message.

Once your team joins the regular calls, listen first. Learn what the group is trying to accomplish. Notice the constraints, the decisions already made, the questions that remain open, and the people who have been carrying the work. That context will show you where help is welcome and where an idea may already have been explored.

After listening and participating, useful opportunities tend to emerge naturally. Your team may have data, implementation experience, a design approach, or a connection that helps the group move forward. Offering that help builds awareness and trust because it responds to a real need.

Leadership can follow later. Project and Steering Committee roles are volunteer positions that carry responsibility to the Community. They make the most sense after someone has established a record of service, judgment, and follow-through.

slides.title: Contributions People Can Use
slides.subtitle: The strongest contribution is useful, shareable, and better when built with others.

cards.title: Technical foundations
cards.body: Specifications, design files, requirements, and reference architectures.

cards.title: Proven practice
cards.body: Tested configurations, best practices, and implementation guidance.

cards.title: Evidence
cards.body: Case studies, success stories, and measurable milestones.

cards.title: Education
cards.body: White papers, seminars, videos, and durable learning resources.

cards.title: Recognition
cards.body: Eligible product and facility recognition aligned with current OCP programs.

cards.title: Collaboration
cards.body: Joint work that brings several organizations into one useful outcome.

slides.transcript:
A contribution doesn't have to be a complete hardware specification or a set of design files. Those are important, but the Community can benefit from many forms of shared knowledge.

A technical foundation might be a specification, a requirements document, a reference architecture, or a design. Proven practice might take the form of a tested configuration, implementation guidance, or a best-practices document. Evidence might be a case study, a success story, or a milestone that shows what worked and what others should know.

Education matters too. White papers, seminars, videos, and structured learning can turn one team's experience into a resource that helps many people. Eligible products and facilities may also pursue recognition through current OCP programs. The exact program details can change, so the durable principle is alignment: connect the offering to approved Community work and follow the current process.

Whenever possible, build with others. A contribution involving several organizations is stronger evidence that the result addresses a shared need rather than one company's promotional goal. Collaborative work is often easier for the Community to trust, accept, and amplify because it demonstrates the behavior OCP is designed to encourage.

The question to ask is not, "What can we announce?" Ask, "What can we share that will help someone solve a problem?" That shift turns expertise into Community value.

slides.title: A Signal of Commitment, Not an Entry Ticket
slides.caption: Current membership family: Startup, Bronze, Silver, Gold, and Platinum.

figure.alt: Current OCP membership tier logos for Startup, Bronze, Silver, Gold, and Platinum.
figure.caption: Current OCP membership tiers. Membership signals commitment; participation and contribution build trust.

entries.text: Membership signals commitment; participation and contribution build trust.

slides.transcript:
Membership is one visible way for an organization to show commitment to the OCP Community. The current family includes Startup, Bronze, Silver, Gold, and Platinum membership. Each level has its own benefits, eligibility rules, and program options, so use the current membership page when you need the details.

The larger point is more important than memorizing a benefit table. Membership is not required to participate in Community projects and workstreams. An organization can attend public meetings, learn, collaborate, and contribute without treating membership as an entry ticket.

If your organization does become a member, use that status as a promise of continued engagement. The logo can signal support, but the Community will still judge the brand by what people do after joining. Are engineers present? Do they listen? Do they contribute useful work? Do they collaborate responsibly?

Membership and participation work best together. The membership mark shows formal commitment. Consistent Community behavior gives that commitment meaning. The resource link takes you to the current OCP membership page so learners always see the latest tiers and benefits rather than a frozen list in this course.

slides.title: The Credibility Flywheel
slides.caption: Listen, participate, contribute, collaborate, earn trust, lead, and keep listening.

figure.alt: Silent animation highlighting each step in a repeating credibility cycle: listen, participate, contribute, collaborate, earn trust, and lead.
figure.caption: Credibility compounds when leadership through service returns to listening.

entries.text: Useful participation becomes a repeatable cycle of trust.
CREDIBILITY COMPOUNDS WHEN YOU KEEP LISTENING
Lead through service—then return to listening.

slides.transcript:
Brand building in an open community works like a flywheel. Each step creates the conditions for the next one, and the cycle becomes stronger with repetition.

Begin by listening. That gives you context. With context, you can participate in a way that is relevant rather than distracting. Participation reveals where your experience can become a useful contribution.

A contribution becomes stronger when you collaborate with other organizations. Collaboration tests the idea against more perspectives and makes the result more useful to the wider Community. When people see your team doing that work consistently, trust grows.

Trust can lead to broader responsibilities. Your engineers may be invited into more complex work, asked to present what they have learned, or encouraged to pursue volunteer leadership. Those opportunities create recognition, but they also create a duty to keep serving the Community.

That is why the cycle returns to listening. A leadership title or a successful contribution doesn't mean the learning is finished. Priorities change. New participants arrive. Better evidence appears.

The flywheel keeps a brand grounded. Listen, participate, contribute, collaborate, earn trust, lead, and listen again. In OCP, credibility isn't a campaign you launch. It is a pattern of behavior that other people experience over time.

slides.title: Trust Is the Brand Asset
items: Treat OCP as a trusted engineering community, not an advertising channel.
Begin in the workstreams that match your organization's expertise.
Listen before deciding how you can help.
Contribute useful work in many possible formats.
Collaborate with others and let leadership follow demonstrated value.
slides.transcript:
The main brand asset in OCP is trust.

Protect that trust by treating the Community as an engineering collaboration, not an advertising list. Start in the workstreams that match your organization's real expertise. Bring the people who can understand the problem, and give them time to listen before proposing an answer.

When an opportunity to help appears, choose the contribution format that serves the need. It might be a specification, a reference architecture, a tested configuration, a case study, a white paper, a video, or an educational resource. The format matters less than the usefulness and integrity of the work.

Build with other organizations when you can. Shared work is more credible, reaches more people, and reflects the open model itself. Let visibility and leadership follow demonstrated value.

If you remember one sequence from this module, remember this: listen, help, contribute, collaborate, and keep showing up. That is how awareness becomes trust, and how trust becomes a durable brand.

choices.feedback_incorrect: A product pitch skips the context and trust that come from listening and useful participation.

questions.feedback_correct: Correct. Listening first reveals the group's needs, relationships, and working style before you decide how to help.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Start by listening in the relevant workstream. Learn the context before offering a solution.

questions.prompt: Which behaviors can build durable trust in the OCP Community? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Contribute a useful case study grounded in real OCP work.
Collaborate with other organizations on a shared problem.
Help a workstream make progress before seeking visibility.
Treat sponsorship as a substitute for participation and contribution.

questions.feedback_correct: Correct. Useful work, collaboration, and service to the workstream create the foundation for earned visibility.

slides.transcript:
Before you finish the module, take a moment to check the order of the trust-building process.

The first question asks what a new organization should do when entering an OCP workstream. The second asks you to identify behaviors that create durable Community trust.

Submit each question once to continue. Correct answers aren't required, and you can retry after reading the feedback. Use that feedback to connect your choices to the core principle: recognition should follow useful participation, not replace it.

slides.transcript:
Nice work. You've completed module one, Earn Trust Before You Amplify.

You now have the foundation: listen in the right workstreams, contribute something people can use, collaborate with others, and let trust build through consistent behavior.

Module two looks at what happens after the work has earned credibility. We'll explore the OCP Marketplace, Summits and Tech Days, communication channels, and OCP Academy. You'll learn how to choose the right way to extend a useful story without turning it into generic promotion.

slides.title: Turn Useful Work into Reach
slides.subtitle: Marketplace, events, education, and communication channels
slides.transcript:
Module two: Turn Useful Work into Reach.

Trust gives your organization something worth amplifying. The next question is where and how to share it.

In this module, we'll look at the OCP Marketplace, the three major Summit families, regional Tech Days, third-party events, and the communication channels available across the Community. We'll also add OCP Academy as a place where expertise can become durable learning.

The goal is not to use every channel. It is to choose the channel that helps the right people understand and use the work.

slides.title: Channels You Will Use with Purpose
slides.subtitle: By the end of this module, you will be able to:
objectives: Choose an OCP channel that fits a specific goal and audience.
Recognize the durable OCP event families and use live event resources.
Apply OCP's newsworthiness filter to potential content.
Build a simple plan that moves from useful work to appropriate reach.
slides.transcript:
By the end of this module, you'll be able to choose an OCP channel with purpose rather than simply asking for more exposure.

You'll understand what the Marketplace does and why qualified discovery can be valuable to Solution Providers. You'll be able to distinguish the major OCP Summits from the smaller regional Tech Days and from third-party industry events.

You'll also compare formats such as the News and Blog, Newsletter, Podcast, Educational Webinars, project workstreams, targeted communications, and OCP Academy.

Most importantly, you'll apply a simple editorial filter. Is the story grounded in real OCP activity? Does it contain evidence, progress, collaboration, or a useful lesson? If so, which channel best serves the people who need it? Those questions will help you turn earned credibility into relevant reach.

OCP Academy: Intro to the Solution Provider Program

slides.transcript:
The OCP Marketplace helps potential adopters discover products, facilities, services, experience centers, and integrated solutions connected to approved OCP work.

Its multi-vendor structure matters. An adopter isn't limited to one company's catalog. The Marketplace brings together approved Solution Providers and a wide range of offerings, so visitors can compare options and find infrastructure that fits a specific need.

For a durable sense of scale, hundreds of members are OCP Solution Providers, and the Marketplace contains around 1,000 listings. Those figures will continue to change, which is why this course uses broad language instead of freezing an exact count.

One statistic from Dirk's presentation remains useful: an average click-through rate of 1.68% to provider sites and contact information. Dirk called out why that result is unusually strong. A typical digital-marketing click-through rate is closer to 0.6%, so the Marketplace rate was about 2.8 times that benchmark. That suggests visitors aren't only browsing. They're qualified people actively looking for a solution and choosing to continue the conversation.

OCP doesn't sell the products. It helps interested visitors find the relevant provider. That makes the quality of the listing important. Clear descriptions, useful detail, appropriate images or videos, and a direct landing page can help a serious visitor understand the offering.

Marketplace participation must follow the current Solution Provider rules. Use the linked program information for the latest eligibility and benefits rather than relying on an older presentation. For a guided introduction, take the linked OCP Academy course, Introduction to the OCP Solution Provider Program.

slides.title: Choose the Stage That Fits the Story
slides.subtitle: Use current event listings instead of relying on a frozen calendar.

cards.title: OCP Summits
cards.body: Global, EMEA, and APAC are the three major Summit families.

cards.title: OCP Tech Days
cards.body: Smaller regional events in Canada, China, Korea, and Singapore, often in the local language.

cards.title: Third-party events
cards.body: Industry conferences where OCP may need Community speakers, workshops, or tracks.

cards.title: Speak
cards.body: Submit useful content during calls for presentations.

cards.title: Host
cards.body: Offer a facility, a date, or a creative Community experience.

cards.title: Sponsor
cards.body: Use sponsorship and exhibits to support a credible story, not replace one.

slides.transcript:
Events give useful work a live setting, but the right opportunity depends on the story and the audience.

OCP has three major Summit families: the Global Summit, the EMEA Summit, and the APAC Summit. These are the largest moments for Community announcements, technical presentations, collaboration, exhibits, and sponsorship.

OCP Tech Days are smaller regional events. They are generally a single day and are often delivered in the local language. Current Tech Day locations include Canada, China, Korea, and Singapore, with Singapore serving the broader Southeast Asia community.

OCP also participates in third-party industry events. The Foundation may host a workshop, contribute a track, join a panel, or need a Community speaker who can explain the work with credibility. If your engineers or project leaders can help, make that interest known.

There are several ways to participate. Submit strong content during a call for presentations. Offer to host an event or a facility tour. Speak, sponsor, exhibit, or propose a creative experience that helps people learn and collaborate.

Dirk's rule for speaking opportunities is wonderfully direct: "Best content wins." Start with the audience's need and the quality of the idea. Because schedules constantly change, use the live Upcoming Events and Past Events pages for current opportunities and examples.

slides.title: Match the Format to the Message
slides.subtitle: Choose the channel that helps the Community understand and use the work.

cards.title: News and Blog
cards.body: Useful stories, milestones, case studies, and guest perspectives.

cards.title: Newsletter
cards.body: Ongoing announcements, events, and Community news.

cards.title: OCP Podcast
cards.body: Human stories, expert conversations, and context that benefits from a voice.

cards.title: Educational Webinars
cards.body: Curated thought leadership with an analyst and a targeted audience.

cards.title: Project Workstreams
cards.body: Focused technical discussion with the people closest to the problem.

cards.title: Targeted Communications
cards.body: Relevant updates for a defined Community segment or geography.

slides.transcript:
The same useful story can take several forms, but each channel creates a different kind of engagement.

The OCP News and Blog works well for milestones, case studies, success stories, and guest perspectives that readers may want to reference later. The Newsletter helps the Community stay current on announcements, events, and ongoing activity. Subscribing is the simplest way to keep that stream connected.

The OCP Podcast gives a story room to breathe. A conversation can reveal the people, decisions, and lessons behind the technical work in a way that a short announcement cannot.

Educational Webinars are a more structured thought-leadership option. The program brings sponsors together with OCP staff and an established analyst to shape a topic around a real market need. The goal is useful, vendor-neutral education, supported by audience interaction and live questions, rather than an hour-long commercial.

Project workstreams remain the closest channel to the technical problem. They are the right place for detailed collaboration, early feedback, and progress that matters to a defined group. Targeted Community communications can then reach a relevant segment or geography when the message has broader value.

Don't choose a format because it is available. Choose it because the format helps the intended audience understand, discuss, or act on the work.

slides.subtitle: Turn hard-won knowledge into durable, accessible learning.

entries.text: can act with more context and confidence

slides.transcript:
OCP Academy adds another important channel: durable education.

The Academy offers free, on-demand learning across open infrastructure topics. Learners can build knowledge on their own schedule, whether they are new to the Community or exploring a specific technology in greater depth. The catalog also includes Community-oriented learning, not only technical courses.

Course availability in multiple languages helps that knowledge travel across regions. Open-source course materials give the Community another way to participate. People can inspect the editable source, suggest improvements, report issues, and contribute updates as the technology or program evolves.

That makes education a meaningful form of contribution. A strong course can preserve the lessons from a workstream, a specification, a deployment, or a Summit presentation. It can help the next engineer avoid repeating old mistakes and arrive at a Community discussion with better context.

Use the main Academy link to explore the full catalog. The OCP Orientation catalog is the best next resource for learners who want detailed help navigating membership, Solution Provider programs, contributions, recognition, procurement, and volunteer leadership. The open-source repository shows how the course materials themselves can be improved.

slides.title: Newsworthy, Useful, and Grounded in OCP Activity
slides.subtitle: A strong story helps the Community understand progress or solve a problem.

cards.title: Project activity
cards.body: Progress from an OCP project, subproject, or workstream.

cards.title: Contributions
cards.body: Specifications, reference architectures, white papers, or other approved work.

cards.title: Evidence
cards.body: Case studies, success stories, and milestones with a useful lesson.

cards.title: Marketplace alignment
cards.body: Products, services, or facilities connected to relevant OCP work.

cards.title: Partnership
cards.body: A collaborative result involving several Community organizations.

cards.title: Not a commercial
cards.body: Generic promotion without Community value does not fit OCP channels.

slides.transcript:
OCP channels are curated. Before asking the Foundation to publish or promote something, test the story against the Community's editorial filter.

The strongest content is grounded in real OCP activity. It may report progress from a project or workstream. It may explain a contribution such as a specification, reference architecture, or white paper. It may show how an OCP-aligned product, service, or facility helped solve a practical problem.

Case studies, success stories, and milestones are especially useful when they include evidence and a lesson that others can apply. Partnerships are valuable because they show organizations collaborating across company boundaries. A story involving several Community members often demonstrates broader relevance than a single-company announcement.

What doesn't fit is a generic commercial. A message that could be sent to any mailing list, with no connection to OCP work or Community needs, doesn't reward the audience for its attention.

Dirk's guidance is a good discipline for any communicator: speak when you have something meaningful to say.

You don't need to fill a posting schedule for its own sake. Bring the Community progress, evidence, and insight.

Then choose the channel that lets that value land clearly. When the story is useful and relevant, amplification has a purpose.

slides.title: One Contribution, Many Useful Touchpoints
slides.caption: Solve a problem, create useful evidence, share it with the right audience, and help the next participant.

figure.alt: Silent animation showing a real problem becoming useful evidence, workstream validation, several possible OCP channels, and value for the next participant.
figure.caption: One credible contribution can travel through events, the Blog, Podcast, webinars, or OCP Academy—chosen by audience and purpose.

entries.text: Choose the place that best serves the audience and the story.
Useful work earns reach. The channel extends its value.

slides.transcript:
One useful contribution can create several touchpoints without becoming repetitive.

The flow begins with a real problem. A workstream identifies a need, and several participants develop an approach. The result may become a contribution, a tested configuration, or a case study with evidence others can use.

Share the work first with the people closest to it. The relevant project community can challenge the assumptions, improve the result, and confirm that the story reflects the shared effort.

From there, choose touchpoints that add something new. An event presentation can invite live questions. A Blog post can preserve the milestone and link to the underlying work. A Podcast can explore the human decisions behind it. An Educational Webinar can teach the market context. An Academy course can turn the lessons into structured learning.

Each format should serve a distinct purpose. Copying the same commercial message everywhere creates noise. Extending the contribution through several useful formats creates a learning path.

The final step points back into the Community. A new participant uses what you shared, joins the discussion with better context, and helps solve the next problem. That is how reach feeds participation instead of distracting from it.

slides.title: Earned Reach Outlasts Advertising
items: Use the Marketplace to make OCP-aligned solutions discoverable.
Choose the event family and participation method that fit the story.
Match the message to the right communication or education channel.
Apply the newsworthiness filter before asking OCP to amplify content.
Let every channel extend useful work rather than repeat generic promotion.
slides.transcript:
Earned reach lasts because it is attached to work the Community can use.

The Marketplace helps qualified visitors discover OCP-aligned offerings and connect with Solution Providers. Events create opportunities to present, host, speak, sponsor, exhibit, and collaborate. Use the major Summits, regional Tech Days, and third-party events according to the audience and the maturity of the story.

Communication channels each have a job. News and Blog content can document progress. The Newsletter keeps people current. The Podcast adds depth through conversation. Educational Webinars support curated thought leadership. Project communications keep technical work close to the people who own it.

OCP Academy turns expertise into reusable learning and gives the Community a way to improve the course source itself.

Across every channel, apply the same editorial test. Is the content newsworthy? Is it grounded in OCP activity? Does it offer evidence, collaboration, or a useful lesson? If the answer is yes, choose the format that best serves the audience. Let the channel extend the value, not replace it.

slides.title: Pick the Right Path
slides.subtitle: Answer each question once to continue. Correctness is not required, and you can retry.

questions.prompt: Your team has a joint case study based on real OCP work. What is the strongest first communication path?

choices.text: Share it with the relevant workstream, then choose an OCP channel that fits the audience and story.
Send a generic advertisement to every available Community channel at once.
choices.feedback_incorrect: Broad promotion ignores relevance and the editorial standard. Start with the workstream and a channel matched to the story.

choices.text: Wait until an event date is printed in a course and use that date indefinitely.
choices.feedback_incorrect: Event schedules change. Use the live event pages and select the opportunity that fits the content.

questions.feedback_correct: Correct. Begin close to the work, then extend the story through the channel that best serves the intended audience.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Use relevance first: validate the story with the workstream, then select the right current channel.

questions.prompt: Which content is likely to meet the OCP editorial filter? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A milestone from an active OCP workstream with a useful lesson.
A collaborative case study involving several Community organizations.
An educational resource grounded in a real technical challenge.
A commercial message unrelated to OCP activity or Community needs.

questions.feedback_correct: Correct. OCP channels favor useful progress, evidence, education, and collaboration grounded in Community activity.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for content that rewards the Community's attention with relevant progress, evidence, or education.

slides.transcript:
This final check asks you to choose the right path from credible work to useful reach.

The first question presents a joint case study and asks what should happen before broad communication. The second asks which kinds of content fit the OCP editorial standard.

Submit each question once to continue. Correctness isn't required, and you can retry after feedback. Look for relevance, evidence, collaboration, and a clear benefit to the Community. Those signals will guide you toward the right answer and the right channel.

slides.thank_you_message: Thank you for completing Module 2: Turn Useful Work into Reach.
slides.cert_message: Identify one relevant workstream, one useful contribution, and one appropriate channel. Then begin by listening.
slides.transcript:
That's a wrap on module two and on How to Build Your Brand in the OCP Community. Thank you for spending this time with us.

You now have a practical starting point. Identify one workstream that matches your organization's expertise. Find one useful contribution your team can make with others. Then choose one channel that helps the right audience learn from that work. Begin by listening.

Use OCP Orientation if you want deeper guidance on navigating the Community, and check the live events pages whenever you're ready to participate in person. Explore OCP Academy for more learning.

If you need help with a brand or communication opportunity, contact Dirk Van Slyke at dirkv@opencompute.org. Keep contributing, keep collaborating, and we'll see you in the Community.
